utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi and Daryl Mundis, assisted by Andres Vatter, our case manager.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the appearances for Defence counsel. They've changed their places.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President, good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this 201st day of the hearings, I'd like to greet everyone present: The Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom. Before we call the witness into the courtroom, the witness who has been waiting for 48 hours now, I would like to point out that the Chamber discussed the motion this morning of the Prosecution -- the Prosecution's motion to reopen its case and to have 50 new documents tendered into evidence. The Chamber, after having deliberated and having taken into consideration the Defence's concerns, is of the opinion - and this is just the Chamber's opinion - that it would not be opportune to file a motion for reopening the case and for admitting the documents into evidence. We don't think that the motion should have these two aspects. We think that there should be one single motion for reopening the case and then subsequently a second motion in the case of a positive decision for the documents. However, the Chamber will not issue any orders with regard to the form and the contents of the motion. It is for the Prosecution to file the motion that they deem appropriate. That is what we are in a position to say at this point in time with regard to the motion in question. There's another issue that concerns the dates. This motion could be filed as of the 23rd of May, which is -- will be the end of the Defence case for Mr. Kubura. However, if the 23rd of May is set as the date, there might be certain delays that concern the Defence's -- because of the Defence's response to the motion, and all this might take some time. We invite the Prosecution to examine the issue with the Defence and to see whether it might be best if this motion were filed immediately at the end of the presentation of the Defence case for General Hadzihasanovic in order to allow for submissions to be made -- written submissions to be made. We invite the Prosecution to consider the matter together with the Defence because we believe the 23rd of May might be a problematic date. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be very brief in order to continue with the witness. If I wasn't clear yesterday, Mr. President - and we have discussed this with the Defence and also in our earlier informal meeting with the Chamber's legal officer - our intention, Mr. President, is certainly to endeavour to file our motion prior to the close of the Hadzihasanovic Defence case. That may or may not be possible due to a number of other factors, including how we're proceeding with respect to that, but we certainly -- if we can't file by the conclusion of the Hadzihasanovic case, were intending on filing immediately before the commencement of the Kubura case. Perhaps if there were to be a week adjournment, we could finalise that motion. Our intention indicating the date of the 23rd would be that would be perhaps an -- an opportune moment for us to physically stand up, tender the documents into evidence, and re-close our case in the event the Chamber allowed us to do that. We also discussed with our learned colleagues the possibility that if -- if we did file as early as possible and the Defence then responded and the Chamber rendered a decision, again perhaps allowing us to reopen, that would then afford the Defence an opportunity to take a position with respect to whether they needed additional time in order to perhaps reopen part of their case to -- to respond to what we have reopened our case on. All the parties, Mr. President, are - I believe - in agreement that -- that this process by which we seek to -- leave to reopen our case should not unduly delay the proceedings in any way whatsoever, which is why we are seeking to finalise our submissions on this as quickly as possible, so that the issue can hopefully be resolved during the course of the Kubura Defence case so that we could smoothly, if we are allowed to reopen -- smoothly move on to that immediately upon the completion of the Kubura case so that we don't have any gaps or any undue delays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this would be -- or we believe that this procedure would be the most appropriate. Could Defence counsel confirm that there are no objections?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good day, Madam Judge. Good day, Your Honour. Defence counsel fully agrees with the approach that the Prosecution has suggested, and as of the time that the motion is filed, we'll try to respond as quickly as possible. Perhaps within two day, 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your cooperation, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There's no objection from our side as to that procedure as outlined by Mr. Mundis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That solves that matter. We'll now call the witness into the courtroom. And as you have requested, the Judges will approach the model as soon as you believe that this is necessary and useful. The trip will only be a trip that will take us a few metres from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General. I'd like to make sure that the equipment is working. Very well. I'll now give the floor to Mr. Bourgon, who will continue with his examination-in-chief. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. Welcome back. We will continue your examination-in-chief concerning your expert report, and I would -- I will begin immediately with question 2 in your statement; however, I would like to ask you that -- because I've read the transcript from the first part -- from our first day together, and if at all possible - and I don't want to stop you from saying everything that you would like to say - but if at all possible, I would ask that you try and shorten your answers. But then again, I don't want to stop you from saying things that you would like to say. Do you understand this procedure?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I begin with question 2, which was provided to you in order to prepare your expert opinion. In this question, you describe the situation in which a senior officer of the Yugoslav National Army assigned to command an army corps in the JNA would find himself before 1990. My first question relates to paragraph 66 of your report, and I would like you to look at paragraph 66 of the report.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: My briefcase is locked. I apologise. I can't see without my glasses, and my briefcase is locked. It's fine now. Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 66. Now, my question is as follows: What you were asked to respond to was the situation of a new army commander at the corps level before 1990, one-nine-nine-zero. Now, I see at paragraph 66 that you mention that in 1987 there were significant reductions of the Territorial Defence, and I also note that in paragraph 86 of your report you mention changes which took place in the JNA in 1988. Now, my question is very short. I would just like to know in what year did the changes to the JNA begin taking place.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The changes in the JNA started soon after the death of President Tito, as far as certain minor issues are concerned. But more significant changes in the JNA started after 1985, and there were radical changes in 1987 or, rather, in 1990 and in 1992. How were these changes manifest? First of all, I must immediately emphasise the fact that the JNA was a constituent part of the Armed Forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was one of the parts of the armed forces together with another constituent part called the Territorial Defence. These two bodies formed the armed forces. The JNA was organised in one way, and the Territorial Defence was organised in a completely different way. Both organisations complemented each other, in terms of the way they functioned in many fields, and they functioned within a certain chain of command and control, and the main objective was the defence of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. They carried out their activities within the system of All People's Defence. The system called All People's Defence and Social Protection. In 1987, up until that time the JNA was organised into six military districts. Roughly speaking, all -- or many, not to say all the military areas, fully overlapped with the territory of the -- the then-Socialist Republics in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now, General, most of these changes are described in your report. What I would like to know precisely is whether there is a link between the changes which took place between 1987 and the aggression, which took place in Bosnia in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to focus on that period. In 1987, the JNA was reorganised. In the military areas -- in the six military areas, there were changes and a new organisational structure was introduced, and three military areas were organised, composed of corps; whereas, previously the military areas had divisions. What was at stake? The following was at stake: There was a desire to eliminate the military areas that more or less covered the territory of the socialist republics at the time by forming three military areas, the first military area in Belgrade, the second in Skopje, and the third one in Zagreb. In order to ensure that the zone of responsibility of those military areas overlapped with at least two or three territories of the republics; that is to say, of regions. The reason was that the commands of various military areas might have fall under the political influence of the republican leaderships, and that would have certainly had an adverse effect on the ideas that the Belgrade regime headed by Slobodan Milosevic had at the time. By organising these military areas, at the same time a process of reducing the Territorial Defence commenced, which was the second component of the Armed Forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. How was this reflected? It was reflected in the following manner: In fact, the Territorial Defence, in terms of mass defence against an aggressor, was the most numerous force. So they attempted to reduce the forces, especially in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They attempted to reduce the number of men within the Territorial Defence and the number of units from the lowest-level units to the highest-level units. It constituted the Territorial Defence. In my report, I provided precise information on the numbers of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. men and on the numbers of units. Among other things, I provided certain examples, in particular an example in Travnik, where in the last three or four years, just before the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was a drastic reduction in the number of men in the Territorial Defence and in the number of units, and an attempt was even made to reduce the force by over 50 per cent. The other reason for which the TO was reduced is as follows: Contrary to the JNA as a constituent part of the forces commanded by the Supreme Command in Belgrade through other subjects within the chain of command -- well, contrary to this system, the Territorial Defence functioned in a different way. In terms of its organisation, the Territorial Defence of republics and regions weren't organised at a level above republics or regions. The highest level of organisation was the Republican Staff of the Territorial Defence in republics as well as in regions. However, in the chain of command, in the case of war the Territorial Defences of republics and regions would execute the orders and decisions of the Supreme Command of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia from Belgrade, and it is evident that with the last reorganisation of the Armed Forces of the SFRY and the JNA - I've explained this in detail in my report - when this force was reorganised, there were reduces in the TO and in the chain of command in the Territorial Defence in republics and regions. The Republican Territorial Defence and the Regional Territorial Defence were placed under that direct command of military areas by order from Belgrade, and the District Staffs in republics and regions and lower-level TO organisations were placed under the command of lower JNA bodies, in military areas, under corps command, brigade command, et cetera. By virtue of this -- by doing this, Belgrade wanted to eliminate the possibility for republican political bodies to exercise their authority in accordance with the Constitution of the SFRY up until that point in time. If you also bear in mind the following fact: That at the same time that the Armed Forces of the SFRY were being reorganised, the TO was being reorganised and it was -- the number of its men were reduced -- if you add to this fact the fact that by order from Belgrade Territorial Defences in republics and regions were being totally disarmed - and I was an eyewitness as a member of the JNA of this event at that point in time in Ljubljana, in Slovenia - on that occasion in Bosnia and Herzegovina - and this was not the case in the other republics, in Slovenia, Macedonia and Croatia and Montenegro in particular - it drew the shortest straw because the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what was then the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- if we're talking about the other two elements that formed the Territorial Defence - that was the Bosniak constituent part and the Croatian constituent part of the Territorial Defence of the Socialist Federative Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina - this body was disarmed 100 per cent. Orders were issued from Belgrade in May 1990, and as a result the JNA used force and took political measures to take all the weapons and ammunition from warehouses and to place them in the locations that suited them, locations in the eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the central part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, around Banja Luka and in a wider area. All of this together, if we look at it in the military sense, in my opinion sends the very persuasive message that all this was done in preparation of the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I'd like to move on to paragraphs 146 to 167 of your report. In these paragraphs, you describe the situation of a senior officer assuming the role of corps commander, that is, before all of the changes you have just described. In these paragraphs, you mention that such a corps commander could benefit from the principle of All People's Defence and social self-protection. You mentioned that the armed forces were part of a common chain of command from the state level to the smallest unit. You mentioned that there were large quantities of weapons, that weapons and ammunition factories were functioning, that there was a combat resupply system in place. You also cover the existence of a very detailed mobilisation system. You mentioned that there were training plans and contingency plans in place. You say that the corps commander would have been a major general with all the necessary training and all the necessary exercises. You mention that such a major general would have complete information on the structure and the composition of his corps. You talk about the major general receiving a specific role and a mission, that he would be told exactly who his commanding officers were, and that he would receive maximum support from the state, the political, and the military bodies. Now, with all of this, my question to you is the following: With such support, in your opinion, I take it that it must have been easy to be a corps commander at that time.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be a commander of an operative unit, that is, a corps, for instance, at the time of the Yugoslav People's Army, meant the following: This corps commander, when the time comes to take over his duties as corps commander, he must have held a wide range of duties from platoon commander upwards to reach the level of the corps commander. To reach that position, he must be of a certain age and he must have the rank that you mentioned. If we compare that with the 3rd Corps, the 3rd Corps commander would have needed another six to eight years, according to the Rules of Service in the JNA, to be appointed to that position in the army. Secondly, when a corps commander is appointed in the JNA, for a long period prior to that appointment he is told that he would be appointed and he engages in preparations for taking over such a highly responsible position. Then sufficient time is given, one month or several months, for the takeover of duty, because it is prescribed that several months are needed for the corps commander to fully take over his duties. It's not sufficient to take your seat at your desk in an office, have a cup of coffee, and sign a piece of paper. What did this takeover of duty mean? It required familiarising oneself with the overall structure of the corps, meeting all the senior officers from the corps command staff to the brigade staff, then familiarising oneself with all the plans, plans of mobilisation and training plans; learning about all the various locations, from the location of personnel to resources and everything else; the line-up of units at the level of brigades, and the introduction of the corps commander to the brigades; his presentation, et cetera, et cetera. When all these things have been done, it is only then that a document is signed whereby a new commander takes over duty from the previous commander. Every corps in the Yugoslav People's Army meant the following: It meant that it had the necessary organisation and structure that had been fully prepared in advance, that the organisation and structure of the corps from the corps command to the lowest-level soldier was up to establishment in strength. Also, the corps commander appointed to that duty has to have the necessary educational background, to have the necessary rank and a certain number of years of experience, and this applied to the lower levels as well, his -- his deputies and all the other senior officers. All of them were appointed in this way, right down to the lowest level, precisely as required by establishment. And the people appointed to those positions had to have the professional qualifications that were required for that position. Furthermore, all the corps units were deployed in various locations, in barracks. All the men were living together. And the location of weapons and ammunition had to be close by to the personnel of all those corps units, and all the legal regulations in force were valid, and even before the corps commander took over his duty, they were being observed. All mobilisation and training plans already are there. The commander just has to familiarise himself with them. And finally, the necessary logistics in the most general sense has been established, because this is an enormous mechanism and as such it is functioning. Once the commander takes over his duty, together with his corps command and all his subordinates in the chain of command, simply has to continue working, controlling, and commanding his units. And my last comment in response to this question: If, shall we say, there would be an external attack against the former Yugoslavia, such a corps commander would have all this available to him, absolutely everything. His duty is to control and command according to the chain of command, and everything else would already be in place, would already be ensured for him. The state would be functioning and the whole defensive system of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would be in the service of that commander. They would provide him everything he needed. And in wartime conditions, needs are extensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If I go on with your report, in paragraphs 168 to 314 you describe all of the changes which took place in the structure of the armed forces, as well as the initial steps which were taken to defend the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And applying these changes to the situation of General Hadzihasanovic, from your knowledge of the evidence I would like to have your opinion on a few of the issues which you raised. And the first issue is at paragraph 323, where you say that the corps did not exist. Can you briefly say what you mean by the fact that the corps did not exist.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the enormous political and military antagonisms that developed in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1990, we are more or less familiar with what happened in that period of time, especially with the other republics of the former Yugoslavia. I wish to point out straight away that unlike all the other republics, Bosnia and Herzegovina, as one of those republics, had the most specific position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, maybe my question is not precise enough. I would just like to know -- you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be short.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- at paragraph 323 that the corps did not exist when he was assigned -- when General Hadzihasanovic was assigned as its commander. What do you mean by "the corps did not exist"?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and be brief with -- and leave out the introduction. On the 8th of April, 1992 a new Territorial Defence was established as the defence force or the new internationally recognised State of Bosnia and Herzegovina. During the summer of 1992 -- I touched the matter the day before yesterday when speaking about the situation in Sarajevo, that is, how the initial period of the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina developed during those first months of aggression against it. As it soon became clear that the system was not functioning - and I think I explained the situation in Sarajevo well - the situation was no better in the area of Central Bosnia and the decision was made to form corps. The decision was made by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When talking about corps, this was just dead letter and paper; that is, the piece of paper where the Presidency said that four corps should be formed but that was rarely available. People scattered all over the area of Central Bosnia, organising themselves on a voluntarily basis to form all kinds of small groups and units who tried in that initial period to organise the defence of their street, their village, and their town. In certain municipalities, there were Municipal Defence Staffs. There was the District Defence Staff in Zenica as well. However, due to the fact that with the beginning of the aggression, that is, in April and onwards, there was a total break-up of the organisation and structure of the Territorial Defence which had existed until then, and as such it could not be put on its feet through any kind of mobilisation documents. Suffice it to say that two-thirds of the total personnel, including the Serb and Croatian population, who were also part of the system, part of the defence, had left. And it was impossible to revive a system if one-third of it is left only. Such a system is considered a total failure, and that is what happened in this case. And when General Hadzihasanovic was assigned the task to form the 3rd Corps in the area of Central Bosnia, he literally had to start from scratch. He had none of the things that I referred to in answer to your previous question which he should have had and which he would have had had he been appointed corps commander in the former JNA. He didn't have organised personnel. He didn't have any plans. He didn't have any officer cadres. I think that he lacked 90 per cent of those things; in some cases, 100 per cent. He had no organised logistics. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. All he had was the order to go to Central Bosnia with a couple of men to somehow find his way to organise and form the 3rd Corps, and his prime task was to defend the country and liberate territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. At paragraph 324 of your report, you go over the fact that there was no existing corps command which would have allowed General Hadzihasanovic to benefit from the experience of qualified personnel. You also underscore the fact that only 3 per cent of the Territorial Defence were professional officers coming from the JNA. Now, I would like to read you a question which was asked to Lieutenant General Roderick Cordy-Simpson from the United Kingdom, and I would ask you to comment on his answer. The question which was asked to General Cordy-Simpson was the following: "What is the advantage for a commander of having a strong headquarters or a command element to perform his duties?" His answer was: "Clearly the need to have a headquarters that reacts quickly in a situation that is as volatile as it was in Bosnia and Herzegovina is absolutely essential, having a headquarters that can operate under such pressure is of paramount importance. I was very lucky. I had a number of officers that I knew well, a number of soldiers that I knew well from my time in the Northern Army Group who I could rely on and trust and they could get the headquarters and implement my orders very quickly. It allowed me to integrate the new members of the staff which came from France, Canada, and Spain; in other words, the contributing nations that were not in the Northern Army Group. I was allowed to get them into the headquarters in a way that they quickly were able to adapt to their new responsibilities; in other words, we were able to plug them into the team rather than everyone coming in from different areas trying to find out who was good, who was weak, and who was better, and who wasn't." Can you comment on this answer from General Cordy-Simpson?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: For any senior military leader, of decisive significance is to have good-quality professional team members, people who are working closely with him and who constitute together with him the corps command. Regardless of the quality of the corps commander, even if he -- if he is the best-possible commander, if he doesn't have a good team in his command, the success of his mission will depend. On the other hand, if you have a good team, one can expect success. And I fully agree with those comments that you have just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My next question deals with paragraph 328 of your report, that is, three-two-eight, where you highlight the fact that General Hadzihasanovic when taking over the corps did not have any existing plans or existing contingency plans. How would that affect his work? And can you explain a bit more what would be the impact of such a situation?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a soldier, and looking at things after so many years, many steps that I myself took during that same war, I was less fearful in those days. Then now, when I see how complex and the conditions and the circumstances under which we worked, they make me fearful, not because of the consequences but what could have happened without me as a human being and as a commander being able to do anything about it. So under such circumstances, as you have described, it is very difficult to expect any serious success. I know that this sentence is so concrete and exclusive and one may ask: How come then we managed to survive and defend the country? Thanks exclusively to enthusiasm, personal ingenuity and ability, hard work, and the struggle for survival, the survival of one's family and one's own. And that was the motto. So people started from nothing and went on from one day until the next waging the struggle, preparing plans, and getting better and better organised as time passed, until the time when the corps was formed. So it is enough to say that there was no corps before that. So he couldn't have had any plans, mobilisation, training, or use-of-forces plans in that initial period, and this applies to 1992 and most of 1993. Things were done -- run to one side, run to another, prevent the breakthrough of the enemy, try ensure logistics without any real plans, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to move on to paragraph 351 of your report, where you conclude as to everything that was missing to allow General Hadzihasanovic to perform his duty and to exercise his command. Now, instead of having you come back on your own conclusion, I would like to ask you to comment on something that was said by General Cordy-Simpson again. Now, the question was: "Could you provide your opinion on the situation in which the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina 3rd Corps in Central Bosnia, what situation it was in and especially the challenges faced by its commander due to the situation?" His answer was: "Yes. I mean, they were a new corps of various disparate units facing an enormous challenge. The first challenge, of course, was a major attack from the north by the Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs, all down from Travnik, Turbe, Jajce, and all that area there. The second challenge they faced was that they were, of course, isolated in Central Bosnia. The Serbs had interior lines of communication back to Belgrade to keep - to Serbia - to keep themselves re-supplied. The HVO also had interior lines of communications to keep themselves re-supplied from Croatia with food, people, weapons, et cetera. The 3rd Corps had no such advantages. In fact, they had every disadvantage. They were cut off, food, ammunition. Weapons once used or lost could not be replaced. Therefore, in every way they had a major military disadvantage over the other two factions involved in this conflict. In addition, unlike my headquarters who arrived on the ground trained, people knowing each other, they had no such advantage, having not had a proper corps before." And asked what kind of challenge this would place on the commander of the corps, General Cordy-Simpson went on to say, "I would suggest to you it placed an enormous challenge on him and I -- and one that I certainly would not have liked to have placed on my shoulders." Can you comment on this opinion of General Cordy-Simpson in light of your own conclusion at paragraph 351 of your report.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that I mostly fully agree with this comment, and the situation was even more complex than the situation described. With regard to the 3rd Corps, reference was made to logistics at one point. Within the entire defence system in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and in 1993, instead of the 3rd Corps and/or other corps receiving supplies from the defence system behind which the state was, the 3rd Corps had to do as best it could on its own and had to supply bodies that were supposed to supply the corps. I don't know if this might be the best and most appropriate example, but in 1994 the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina asked me whether we might lose the airport in Sarajevo, whether that was possible. As I had to answer this question very seriously -- I had to take this question very seriously, I answered in simple terms. I said, "Since I know what my corps is like, if I was in Mladic's and Karadzic's position, I'd take it in a few days' time." That scared him, because if that were to happen, that would have been the end of Bosnia and Herzegovina. All he said was, "What can we do?" And I said, "I need quite a lot of anti-armour shells. I need a few anti-armour laser weapons" that were to be placed on Mount Igman, that is above the airport, et cetera. And he said, "Well, I can't help you with that." That shows what the situation was with regard to logistics. That shows how supplies were obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would now like to show you a few annexes from your report and ask you some questions on these annexes, moving on briefly. And I will start with Annex 56 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you press the third button, "Computer evidence," you'll see the annex on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Do you see, General, Annex 56 of your screen?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you briefly describe what this is.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This annex shows the territory --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, if I may, you can use the pencil that is on the table and you may actually draw, if you want -- if you need to indicate some things on this slide, if that is necessary. But I'd like to go quite briefly, because there's quite a number of slides to go through. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Bosnia and Herzegovina. The black lines are the borders of the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the number of municipalities that there were at the time. The colours used in fact show the first organisational order issued by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This order was issued and the order was issued to organise the corps within the army in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Five corps were established and organised in that order. The 1st Corps in Sarajevo -- it had its headquarters in Sarajevo. The 2nd Corps, with its headquarters in Tuzla. The 3rd Corps, with its headquarters in Banja Luka -- or rather, in Zenica. The 4th Corps, with its headquarters in Mostar. And the 5th Corps, with its headquarters in Bihac. The 3rd Corps is depicted in green, and it shows the territory covered by its zone of responsibility in the central part of Bosnia. It shows how far to the north of Bosnia and Herzegovina it extends, in the direction of Croatia, in the direction of the River Sava. I think it's clear enough. It's not necessary to draw anything on this image. That is the first time the corps in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were formed, in August 1993 -- or I apologise, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to move now to Annex 59. And if you can explain exactly what is meant by "grouping tasks" that were given to General Hadzihasanovic and what are -- what was your objective in preparing this annex?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to use this annex to show the municipalities that were then in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. They have been listed here: Zenica, Bugojno, Busovaca, and all the other municipalities, Donji Vakuf, Gornji Vakuf, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Travnik, Zavidovici, Zepce, Jajce, and then Breza, Ilijas, Vares, Fojnica, Kresevo, Kiseljak, Hadzici, Visoko, Maglaj. In the middle, where it says "municipalities," you have the municipalities listed that at the time weren't under the control of the 3rd Corps. What did I want to show by using this annex? I wanted to show - and I have done so - that -- I wanted to show what was essential in all the municipalities. I wanted to show which units had to be established on the basis of the first idea -- the initial idea for structuring these forces. All the men had to be visited, controlled. You had to deploy them in certain areas. You had to regulate matters by issuing plans and tasks. They all had to be placed under someone's command, within an organisational entity called the 3rd Corps of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, if you would like to use the electronic pencil, there are three buttons, and you can use three colours: Red, green, and blue, which are at the top of your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for the sake of everyone present in the courtroom, I'd like to point out that we have an English version for all of the annexes which was distributed with the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Annex 61. If you can describe what Annex 61 was and what you wanted to show with this annex.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to use this annex to show how the 3rd Corps was initially to be structured, and it indicates the order issued by the Supreme Command Staff and the date of the order when this structure was to be established. Colours have been used to indicate certain units. For example, units of various kind have been indicated, and this colour shows that all mechanised brigades are concerned. This colour is used for mountain brigades. This colour is used for motorised brigades, et cetera. And it shows the organisational structure initially planned for the 3rd Corps of the ABiH. The first two rows consist of brigades. In this row, in these rectangles, you have the logistic bases. Then you have the Military Police Battalion, anti-aircraft unit, an independent unit for anti-sabotage action, a centre for training recruits, and a Municipal Defence Staff in Zenica. And the last row, in green shows units attached to the staff. For example, an engineering company, a communications company, and a company for electronic jamming.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, you mentioned that this is the plan as of November 1992. How would you qualify this plan as of that date based on the reality? Was it possible? Was it a dream? Or was it impossible? What is your opinion on this?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, when the 3rd Corps commander received the order to form the corps in this manner, I don't believe he had any of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these units indicated. Most of those units only existed on paper. What was to be done? Together with his officers from his command, from the corps command, and with others, he had to go into the field. From the north, from Maglaj, towards the west, towards Bugojno. It was necessary to keep moving and from -- and to keep going from place to place. It was necessary to become familiar with the units that were in the Central Bosnian area at the time. It was necessary to speak to members of the units. And by way of an example: 10 or 15 companies scattered around villages, towns, it was necessary to speak to them and to integrate them within, for example, one of these brigades. It was necessary to enlarge these units and form what has been depicted here. That's an example, but that concerns all the units that have been depicted here as part of the structure of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now, you have described in your report the changes which took place from after 1990 until 1993 but -- and many witnesses have also talked about these changes. Now, what I would like to do is if you could look at this annex, which is 62, and describe what were the relationship between the various organs as the armed forces moved from the Territorial Defence to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I guess you have three annexes that speak about that. This is the first one, 62. I'd like you to look at this one. Maybe, General, if you can start by the top, where we see kind of a yellow semicircle or a circle and say what this is and what are the relationships and the different colours on this annex.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first diagram shows the following: We can see how the defence for the state was organised, the entire system for defence. There are many bodies and various links between all these bodies. At the bottom, there are two full lines: A black and red one, and this is used to indicate the line of command and control; and the dotted line is the line of diagonal influence and command. On the left hand, it says: "The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina," which is the Supreme Command. At the same time, to the right there is one large circle and four smaller circles within that large circle. There's the General Staff -- the Main Staff -- the General Staff which was in the process of transformation from 1992 to 1994, and you have the years when it was transformed from the Supreme Command Staff to the General Staff. To the left, in grey, you have the Presidency, the government, the Ministry of Defence, the Presidency of a canton -- or rather, district, district government, district secretariats for National Defence. And then we go down below, towards the municipal level we have the same at the level of the municipalities. You have the organisation and the structure of the authorities exercising power at that time in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Beneath the General Staff, the colour orange was used to indicate that this was still the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was no Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, whenever you indicate or mention a body, could you put your pen on the name of the body. When you say "the Presidency," could you please point to it with your pen so that we can follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Ministry of Defence, the District -- or rather, Cantonal Presidency. They're governments. The District Secretariats for National Defence, in the cantons -- or rather, regions. The Presidency of municipalities, municipal councils, and the Municipal Secretariat for Defence. Here we have the Supreme Command Staff in 1992, then its transformation into the Republican Staff of the Territorial Defence. And then the Main Staff of the Supreme Command and then the General Staff of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 1994 to 1995. Taken all together, this is the main command of the Territorial Defence -- or rather, of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This entire part here, in this colour, all these units contained here consist of certain units and brigades. I'm now underlining these units here. These units are directly linked to the main command, the General Staff. Then we have subordinate units below the main command. We have the District Territorial Defence Staff. Linked to these staffs, we have the Municipal Territorial Defence Staffs and all these units here. Then there are the Municipal Defence Staffs linked to their own units. This first diagram shows that this was the Territorial Defence. In the summer of 1992, there was no ABiH. We could move on to the next diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Before you move on, General, to your second one, I have a very short question: What is the difference between command and control and diagonal influence and command?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell you what command and control means. "Command and control" is an idea that encompasses many measures, activities, and steps through which one leads a military unit. Command and control, we have two words here: "Command" -- or rather, "control" is a more complex word. It has to do with a higher level of military units, at the operative level and above. If we look at command and control from the level of the state and then right down to the bottom, to the lowest-level unit, then one could say that control is what one sees in the work of the Supreme Command and in the General Staff and in the corps command as you go down the chain of command toward -- down the chain of command, command is more present and control is not so present or not to the same extent. We say that in a platoon or a company, there is no control; you just command. The commander of a company or a platoon orders his troops to do such-and-such a thing. As you go up the chain of command, then control is something one encounters more frequently, since this is a wider and more complex concept. If I may elaborate on this. I'll try to draw a scheme -- I'll just divide this rectangle in this way: At the top you have in fact the Supreme Command, command number 1, the most senior command. At the bottom, you have the lowest-level unit; for example, a platoon. That's the lowest-level unit. As you go from top to bottom, well, this would be control here. From the highest command level to the lowest level. And as you go down, as you descend, control becomes less and less present. But here, when we go up from the lowest level unit, this would be command. As you go up toward the Supreme Command, depending on the level, this becomes less and less present.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I'd just like to confirm one thing with you. And because I know that I went through this discussion with an interpreter before with the fact that you have -- the words "command" and "control" are very similar, I would just like you to explain: The top part in your diagram, is that command and then the lower part is control? Can you confirm? Because in the interpretation in the transcript, it seemed to be the other way around. Which one is at the top and which one is at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the top, you have what we call "rukovodjenje," control. And at the bottom, that would be "komondovanje," command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now move on to the second slide. Can you explain which changes took place between 1992 and 1993 that are illustrated on this annex.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this diagram, we have the left vertical depicted, from the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina down to the municipalities. It's identical to what was depicted on the previous -- in the previous diagram. But -- and this part is also identical. But here in blue you have the Main Staff of the Supreme Command. The colour used to depict it in fact shows that the corps of the ABiH were formed and all these units, and it shows how much it was necessary to transform, how many units had to be transformed from the Territorial Defence into the ABiH. That's this part that I have just encircled. These are also units attached to the General Staff. Then you have the corps and all the units under the corps, all the units linked to the corps. Here, in the right part of the diagram, you can see what remain from the previous diagram, because in the previous diagram all of this was also in blue, but there's part of the Territorial Defence that has remained; namely, the Regional Territorial Defence Staffs, units attached to them; then the Municipal Territorial Defence Staffs, and units attached to the Municipal Territorial Defence Staffs. These dotted lines indicate that -- given the overall situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time which body could influence certain other bodies and the extent to which it was possible to influence other bodies. In a normal military organisation, this is not necessary. It's not necessary to have such dotted lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We have a few minutes just to go quickly over the next annex, and then I think we will be ready for the technical break. Can you explain what the next annex, which is 64, and what has -- what has happened from 1993 until 1994 and what was happening to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third annex follows on the previous annex, and it shows that from the first annex all that has remained is -- is this, only this part of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Everything else is the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But the title of the annex is "The end of 1993 and 1994." And during that period of time, we still had this number of Territorial Defence units. It's true that they had almost -- they had almost disappeared entirely, but they were still in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... technical difficulty. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I repeat what I was saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but quickly, because we need to go for the technical break.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This third annex in fact shows, if we bear in mind the first annex we had, which depicted the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the beginning of 1992 -- here in the title of this annex, it says "in 1993 and 1994." Of the Territorial Defence, this is all that remained. Only these units in this colour. And afterwards, these units were disbanded too, and thus the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been completely reorganised and established.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how important is it to understand these command and control and diagonal lines of influence -- how is it important to understand these relationships in order to have full knowledge of the position in which General Hadzihasanovic was in in 1993. So this will be my first question when we return from the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's quarter to 4.00 and we will resume at about ten past 4.00, quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, I did mention to you what my next question was. Can you please look at this Annex 63 of your report. Now, looking at this annex, and I'd like you to focus on the middle, where you have the -- the corps of the army. Can you draw a circle around where the corps of the armies are.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, can you -- from where the corps are, we see that we have a direct line coming down from the Main Staff of the Supreme Command. Can you also circle this, the full line.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are there any other lines that were supposed to command or to issue orders to the corps?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't any, and there shouldn't be any.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at all the other lines, the dotted lines - and there are various types of dotted lines - and these are coming from the War Presidency, coming from the Presidency, coming from the government, and also coming from other organisations which are indicated in green. What would be the impact of these various lines of influence on the work of the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be put in one word. In the military organisation, in the structure of a unit, all these other lines are unnecessary, that is, all the dotted lines. Only the full lines are needed. All these other lines that you have referred to indicate influence, which at a certain point in time can only be harmful for the corps commander and can only be a cause of problems for him. Depending on those influences and how great they are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and with respect to which issues, they aggravate and complicate the task of control and command for the corps commander, and he had very little influence over them in wartime. Let me give you an example, my own example from the war in 1994, when a Chief of Staff in municipality Centar, Huso Kamberovic. While I was on the defence line, my driver heard on the radio that he was giving 20.000 German marks to a deputy commander of one of my brigades in Sarajevo. This is this horizontal influence or diagonal influence, which is sometimes used to improve somebody's personal position and status or protect that position, yet it could be the head of a municipality, the president of a district, or anyone else. In this case, this municipal leader wanted to have my brigade commander linked to him. And as I didn't have sufficient funds or logistics and the Chief of Staff in the municipality did, he is offering it directly to my brigade commander, which is quite unacceptable and has absolutely no excuse, viewed from a military standpoint. If a municipal leader has certain needs with respect to units, then he has to achieve it through the corps command and its bodies. The corps commander and his bodies. In wartime, what this boils down to is to the buying of people, and this was widespread in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to move to a different topic, which has to do with Annex 65 of your report, dealing with displaced persons. In this annex, can you explain what you wanted to picture. Annex 65. What you wanted to picture in this annex. And can you briefly explain for the Judges what that means.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This annex shows the following: The title is "Persecution and migration of the population in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps." This is a topographic military map that has been scanned and the following information has been provided on it: For example, this is the municipality of Maglaj. This is Teslic, the municipality of Visoko, Kiseljak, Fojnica, Tomislavgrad, et cetera. I can't see too well to be able to read all the names. At the same time, this annex, with the small and large circles in different colours, indicate the ethnic structure of the population in the area at the time. There's a legend in the bottom right-hand corner. The blue are the Bosniaks. The yellow is for the Croats, and the red for the Serbs. On the basis of a large number of sources which can be considered reliable official sources of data, and I use them, including data of the International Red Cross and many other sources, as indicated in my report. We see that all the municipalities outside the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps but not the first area of responsibility according to which it spread up to the River Sava, but the territory that was actually controlled by the 3rd Corps shows how many Bosniaks and Croats had fled from neighbouring municipalities and were concentrated in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, which it in fact controlled. And all these directions indicate from where these people came and in what numbers, from which municipalities these people had fled and had been expelled, and found refuge in the territory of Central Bosnia. In my report, you will see tables with the actual figures for each municipality and the population on the basis of the 1991 census. According to that census, the calculations were made so as to see that tens of thousands of refugees had fled from neighbouring municipalities and found shelter in Central Bosnia in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, fleeing from the Serb aggressor, and later in 1993 this becomes even more complicated with the outbreak of the open conflict with the HVO. So things become complicated to the extreme. My conclusion is that this just shows how complicated the situation was and how difficult it was for the corps commander, regardless of the fact that certain political and civilian entities endeavoured to do something for the refugees who were pouring in, all this was very little. The greatest responsibility fell on the corps commander. Why? Due to a fundamental fact, and that is that all those displaced persons were close or distant relatives of his soldiers. So whatever was happening during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was related to family relationships between soldiers and members of their families. And in view of this highly complicated situation in 1992 and 1993, because a defence system was not functioning fully, it was necessary to find the time, the resources, and the manpower to identify the able-bodied men for military service among the displaced persons, among these refugees, to register them, to call them in for interviews, to assign them to units, to train them to a satisfactory degree, and to send them to join units in combat activities. This was a very complicated undertaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just a question concerning your answer. You mention at line 13 that the greatest responsibility fell on the corps commander. Are you referring to a legal responsibility, or are you referring to the fact that the refugee situation created problems for the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the latter. And in what I have just said, I have tried to explain that because those refugees were causing problems not through their own free will but the very fact that they were so numerous and that they needed to be provided with accommodation and food and the able-bodied had to be found and mobilised and sent to units, all this caused vast problems for the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, I'd like to move on to another topic, which is Annex 73 of your report. But before I do so, I'd like to ask you one quick question: How much did you know about the situation in Central Bosnia in 1993 when you were the corps commander in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I knew very little. I personally during 1993 don't think I saw the 3rd Corps commander once or twice. We may have spoken on the phone once. That was the reality of the situation, resulting from the fact that for all of four years I was continuously day and night either on the lines or in my units or on wheels. I was constantly on the move. I slept wherever I could. I ate where I could. When someone gave me something as the corps commander, trying to deal with numerous duties I had on the move. I am saying this because it shows that I didn't have time to follow the situation elsewhere. But I can't say that I didn't know anything. Up to a degree I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you describe what is Annex 73 of your report, and especially what is pictured by the red line in the middle, as well as the blue part.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This annex is, again, a picture of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with two areas in two different shades of blue. The darker blue area, including the part in the north, actually shows the already-formed three Croatian communities under the name of Herceg-Bosna, the largest, consisting of 13 municipalities, formed on the 18th of November 1991, and it included all of this south-east, as far as Zenica, and Zenica is here. Then a second Croatian community, known as Central Bosnia, consisting of four municipalities; that is to say, Maglaj, Zepce, Zavidovici, and Zenica. And a third Croatian community, of Posavina, Bosnian Posavina, which included eight municipalities: Derventa, Bosanski Brod, and so on, as far as Brcko. The lighter blue colour in the central part delineated with a red line is the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and their effective control. And what I wanted to show here was, as can be seen on this slide, that the entire area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps of the BH army covered a territory which the Croatian people had already proclaimed to be their own, and this was the cause of all subsequent problems and conflicts between the 3rd Corps and the HVO in Central Bosnia. And in these three Croatian communities in Bosnia, we also see their military divisions. Here in the south is the operative zone jugo istok, or south-east; the operative zone north-west; the operative zone Central Bosnia; and in the north, operative zone Posavina. And heading the Central Bosnia zone was Tihomir Blaskic, and in this operative zone, because they are close to the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility, the commander was Stjepan Stiljek, if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, if I understand you correctly, the complete area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps was also the area of responsibility of the HVO. Am I correct in saying this?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General Hadzihasanovic, as the commander of the 3rd Corps, how many operations -- operative zones of the HVO was he facing, or how many HVO enemies did he have?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This thick black line shows the line of separation between the operative zones in the HVO, and it follows from this that the command of the 3rd Corps had to confront two operative zones of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, if I would add to this same annex the area of responsibility of the Army of Republika Srpska, the VRS, would that also overlap the complete area of operations of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at another annex showing the Serbian Autonomous Regions that had been formed, out of all these municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina only seven municipalities remained for which they didn't have any interest; that is, neither the Serb policies nor the Croatian policies. And this is the municipality in the north-west, the one of -- called Velika Kladusa; the municipality of Cazin; in Central Bosnia, the municipality of Visoko; and the municipality of Breza. These are four municipalities. And in the north-eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the municipality of Srebrenik, Tuzla, and Kalesija. Only these seven municipalities were not a component part of any of the Serbian Autonomous Regions nor of any of the three Croatian Communities of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to move to Annex 110. And I would like you to explain what exactly this -- what is illustrated by this annex. Now, a number of witnesses have testified before this Trial Chamber about the consequences or the strategic plan of the HVO as well as of the VRS in 1992 and 1993. Can you help us understand this annex.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This annex also shows a military topographic map that has been scanned, and on it we see the military situation of all three sides. As stated in the heading, "The deployment of forces of the ABiH, the VRS, and the HVO and of the Croatian army," because this was a time period, that is, July 1993 to March 1994, which is a lengthy period of time during which with brief intervals attempts were being made -- I shall now encircle the places where the HVO and the Croatian army together --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, could you wait just for one second. We -- we lost the slide show. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attempts were being made by the Croatian army and the Croatian Defence Council to occupy Gornji Vakuf and Gornji Vakuf, the town itself, is here, and the town of Bugojno is here. These red arrows show the axis of efforts being made even before this time period to capture these areas, even at the end of 1992 and in January 1993. But this man shows when the most intensified efforts were being made, and that is the dates indicating -- indicated at the top. Why did the HVO want to capture Gornji Vakuf? I'm addressing this purely from the military standpoint. If the HVO and the Croatian army had managed succeeded in occupying Gornji Vakuf along this road marked in yellow which I'm now marking in red, they would have linked up with the HVO in Novi Travnik, and Novi Travnik is right here. What would that mean? That would automatically mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... marking something? Because we don't see the lines. So maybe there is a problem. Sorry. Go on.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am drawing lines. Where it says "3K" just above those -- that number in letter is Novi Travnik. And the dotted line I'm now drawing, behind that line are mountains, very high mountains which separate Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Vitez from Gornji Vakuf, which is here, and Bugojno, which is here. Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno actually in military terms succeeded in their defence by - as I said of Sarajevo - by defending the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the country was defended. But this is from the standpoint of the Serb aggressor. It is also stated in comparison with Sarajevo that by succeeding in defending Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno, Bosnia and Herzegovina had been successfully defended and its division prevented. Because had that happened, Bosnia-Herzegovina would have quickly disappeared most probably. Why? Because the HVO forces would have linked up in Novi Travnik, Vitez, and Busovaca with other HVO forces, and then the 3rd Corps commander would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not have had a theoretical chance of defending the Bila Valley. In military terms, there would have been no chance of success. Shortly after that, Travnik would have fallen and the entire Bila Valley, and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna would have spread as far as Zenica. After that, whether a couple of towns would succeed in their defence was a matter of time. So the Croatian Defence Council pursued this aim constantly, that is, to gain control of the route of salvation that I have drawn, that is, militarily to capture the largest part of their territory, which they considered to belong to the Croatian Community, of course in cooperation and collaboration with the Army of Republika Srpska, and after that they would have agreed how they would have cut up Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a result of which a Greater Serbia would have been formed from the east and a Greater Croatia from the west. The significance of Gornji Vakuf is very great in military terms, that is, defending it successfully was of the utmost importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to move to a different aspect of your report, which is covered in paragraphs 528 to 532, where you explain the levels of command and control as being tactical, operative, and strategic. Can you further explain the importance of dividing command and control relationships in these three levels.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in all armies throughout the world, in the majority of armies, we have these three levels of command and control. This is how everything is structured in those armies. What does this mean? At the strategic level of command and control, we have the Supreme Command of the state, including the Ministry of Defence and the main army command. The operative level of command and control is, in fact, the level of an operative unit that we call a corps, and everything below that level involves the tactical level of planning; that is to say, of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question deals with the exercise of command at the operative level. I would like to have your opinion as to what the focus of a corps commander should be in terms of time. Is a corps commander looking at the battle as it unfolds, or is he looking ahead? And if so, how far ahead and why?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "operative command and control" is a term from which one can derive a concrete military concept, that of operations. This means carrying out operations, planning operations, supervising the way in which an operation is carried out, et cetera. Operations are carried out by a corps. In the course of 1992, 1993, and to a significant extent in 1994, it was only in the middle of 1994 and in 1995 that the corps of the ABiH were actually in a condition to carry out operations, and that in fact is the real task of each and every corps commander. Up until that time, various low-scale attacks were carried out up to the level of a brigade commander. What I do mean by this? A corps commander in this first case I have mentioned is a case in which he is fully involved, in that he plans -- he drafts plans, forwards orders to those who are to execute the plans, et cetera. In all other cases, if we're talking about combat, these are activities that company commanders, battalion commanders carry out, and perhaps brigade commanders. But according to military jargon, this is up to the level of the brigade and within a brigade. In spite of the fact that in 1992 and 1993 there were small-scale fights that -- in which a platoon or two or a company or one to two battalions were engaged in at the most, in spite of this fact, one couldn't say that the corps commander was not present. The corps commander was present but within the chain of command. The corps commander authorises certain combat actions at certain levels. Since all these combat operations, all these fights, are authorised by a brigade commander with the knowledge of the corps commander, this also shows the extent to which he can or should be involved in such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I just -- I did not hear the word you used in your language, but at page 43 at line 9, we see that "authorised by a" -- it says here -- sorry, line 8: "Since all these combat operations." Did you say "operations" or did you use another word?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me -- I'll go back, General. If you can look in the transcript in front of you, page 43 at line 7. It says: "The corps commander authorises certain combat actions at certain levels." And then it says: "Since all of these combat operations, all these fights, are authorised by a brigade commander ..." Now, are we talking about combat operations or combat activities?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terms, you say that the brigade commander authorised combat activities, and lower down the level a battalion commander authorises combat. Because there are three levels of combat, three forms of combat: You have combat, fight, and operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I'd like to move on. I'd like to give you a -- a document. I would like the usher to come and give you this document which I have shown to my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you ask your witness to clarify the distinction between a combat, fight, and operation so that we can be clear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] three levels of fighting as being -- you mentioned three categories. Can you explain the difference between those three categories.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boj, which would be combat, is the lowest level. And the units, together with the battalions, carry this out. I said combat was the lowest level of operations, carried out by units together with the battalion. A platoon, a company, a battalion. A battle is the second level of military activity, carried out by a brigade or a number of brigades -- or rather, by divisions, because there is an establishment between a brigade and a corps. Or to be even clearer, because the term "operative group" has frequently been used here -- but this isn't a permanent formation. Whereas operations, which is the highest level of military activity, operations are something which are carried out by corps and higher level operations, armies or by groups of corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, this distinction between those three categories, of course it would be very important for officers who have military education, but is it possible that the words and the concepts could have been mixed up in 1993 because officers were not well trained, as you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. If someone has no military education, it's very difficult to clarify this to such a person and there would be no purpose in trying to clarify such terms without having previously worked on such matters at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you two more questions with respect to the level of command of a corps commander. And my first question is: Because the commander of a corps works at the operative level, how important is it for him to trust the chain of command at all levels below him right down to the platoon?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also think that in all armies throughout the world the chain of command is the essential component for the way in which each military unit works. As a result, within the chain of command -- and why did I say initially that when units are being formed it's necessary to have plans for bringing units up to strength and it's necessary to assess the men and officers in good time to see who shall be appointed to given posts and a lot of time is always spent on assessing the individuals who should be assigned to senior positions, and this is because it's necessary to have confidence in such men. If there's no confidence in the men, there's no chain of command; if there's no chain of command, there are no units. It's impossible for missions for to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My second question which -- I wanted to read you a quote from General Cordy-Simpson, but somehow I have misplaced this quote. But maybe I'll simply ask the exact same question which I asked General Cordy-Simpson, and that was: In terms of the responsibility of commanders at various levels, it has been said that the higher the level of the commander, the less involvement he has directly with his subordinates and that there is a big difference in how much they can personally influence the actions of their subordinates, depending on the level. Would you agree that -- and General Cordy-Simpson specifically said that "The last level at which a commander is directly in contact with his subordinate is at the battalion level."

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a little confused. What does he mean when he says "his direct subordinates"? At each level of command, it's necessary to have direct contact with one's subordinates. A battalion commander, a brigade commander, a corps commander. That's the chain of command. If you then replace this idea -- the general probably thought that the higher the level of the commander, the less contact he had with the soldiers or the troops. In that case, that's quite correct. He's absolutely right. But a corps commander has his first assistants within his command who are in direct contact with him. He must be in -- or he must have permanent contact with them. And he is also in contact with his immediate subordinate commanders of units. And the corps commander has to have permanent contact with them and he has to work with them on the permanent basis. Everything else is secondary. I don't know if I have been sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have now found the quote, and I will now ask you this, because it looks very much like your answer, but I would like you to comment on this. My question was: "I would like to know, General, if you see a difference between the responsibilities of a battalion commander and the responsibilities of a corps commander towards soldiers and how much of a personal involvement do each of those have." And General Cordy-Simpson replied: "It is my belief that battalion command is the last time an officer will directly influence how his soldiers perform on the battlefield. He is responsible. He is the man they see. He can will them to fight better than any other person in the battalion. Once you become a brigade commander or a divisional commander or a corps commander, that direct influence is lost. As a brigade commander, you tell your battalion commanders what you require them to do but you cannot permanently influence the individual soldiers within that battalion to fight harder, fight better, or anything else. Certainly when you become a divisional commander, you have totally lost that ability to influence the battle of how people fight. And as a corps commander, you are way above that.
