You are directing the battle at the high tactical, I would put it, level but you are not directly influencing how soldiers fight on the ground at that particular moment." Can you comment on this answer from General Cordy-Simpson.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, in fact, confirms what I thought was in question. It concerns the relation between the commander and soldiers. I provided you with my answer. I could expand on it, but I agree with most of what the general said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I move on to a different topic, which is that you raise at paragraph 537 of your report and that we also find in Annex 38. And this deals with the principles of armed combat. Now, what you see on your screen is I just took the headings out of Annex 38 to make it easier for everyone in the courtroom. Now, I know you read English, so maybe you can look at this Annex 38, which is on your screen. I'd like to know how important are these principles and why is it that commanders, and especially a corps commander, should abide by these principles, as you say in your report.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: All senior commanders have to abide by these principles of armed combat. The principles enumerated here are in a certain sense guidelines that show how a unit should be led and how when combat tasks are being carried out the mission assigned should be accomplished. The first principle: "Constant maintenance of a high degree of combat readiness," is in fact a principle that is valid for a corps commander as well as for the last man in the corps and the last soldier. According to this principle, everyone has his own role. Naturally, responsibility is greater as you go up the chain of command towards the corps commander. Naturally, it's the corps commander who has the greatest responsibility. Because there are many questions that have to be dealt with, that have to be borne in mind. It's necessary to plan in good time and ensure that the highest degree of combat readiness is maintained within units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, if you -- I'd like you to -- to try and -- and focus on those principles. But at paragraph 538 of your report, you mention -- you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. talk about the platform which was adopted by the Presidency, and you also say that the three principles which would be the most important ones would be determining the aim, determining the focus, and unity of armed combat. Can you explain what you mean by those three principles being the most important ones.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I didn't quite understand your question. By saying this, I wanted to emphasise that the platform adopted in June 1992 by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina - and it applied to the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina - virtually all these principles of armed combat emanated from that platform, but they were taken over from documents of the Yugoslav People's Army, as we were the successors, and I here tried to highlight these three principles: Determining the aim of the struggle, determining the focus of the struggle, and unity of armed struggle or combat. These are three key principles for armed combat. All three of these principles are fully contained in the platform adopted by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in June 1992. Determining the aim; I'll be brief. When a country enters a state of war, it is essential for the Supreme Command or the Presidency or the Assembly, et cetera, to pass a document, an act, determining the aim of the struggle in clearest terms. If there is any vagueness or lack of clarity or incompleteness regarding the state, its structure, its policies, its population, et cetera, will be reflected in the aim of the struggle. What I am trying to say is that -- that the political leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina, without going into its relationship with international organisations and international factors, has the duty of determining the aim of combat, and in its platform these aims were clearly indicated. Nevertheless, there were three new army -- armies being formed: The Army of Republika Srpska, the Croatian Defence Council, and Fikret Abdic's army, all of which, despite these clear aims from the platform, emerged as opposition to those aims. Now, why, that is a very broad issue, and we are talking about it now, in fact. Now, the second aim is determining the focus of combat, the focus of armed struggle. In the beginning, during 1992, the focus of the armed struggle of the corps of the ABiH was the struggle against the Army of Republika Srpska or, rather, the JNA. And this went on throughout 1992. However, for other reasons - and I am profoundly convinced that this wasn't due to any shortcomings in the platform but, rather, due to different interests on the part of those who did not wish to accept the platform - the Croatian Defence Council was formed, and the focus of the struggle had to be corrected. And then again there's Fikret Abdic and his army and many other problems which affected the choice of the focus of struggle in the defence of the state. And third, the unity of combat -- of armed combat. What is characteristic of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war is that further to the platform adopted by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, after which the political leadership, as well as the military leadership of the country, did everything to avoid the emergence of the HVO -- or rather, its direct opposition to the ABiH and also to avoid Fikret Abdic appearing up. So there were documents signed in Zagreb to the effect that the HVO would retain its name but would join in the struggle for the common goal under the command of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As far as I know, later in August 1992 a decree with the force of law was passed instructing the HVO to place itself under the command of the ABiH in the spirit of the platform and to fight against the Serb aggressor. However, all this did not bear fruit. I'm just saying what efforts were made to ensure unity of the armed struggle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would now like to move to the last section of your report, which deals with, as you call it, "specific events." And I will begin by the section where you -- which is entitled "The mission of General Hadzihasanovic and Brigadier Kubura." And this is at paragraphs 598 to 618. Now, you have already said that the concept of mission was very important. But at paragraph 602, you mention that if the mission fails, the commander will be held responsible by his superiors, and if the mission is a success, the corps commander will also be considered responsible. My first question is the following: When we say that the commander is responsible for the mission, whether it fails or it succeeds, is that different from the responsibility of a commander for the conduct of his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understood your question fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I will say the question again. I'm referring to paragraph 602 of your report. If you can look at paragraph 602, where you mention that the commander of a corps is directly responsible and accountable for the accomplishment of the mission of the corps pursuant to the orders issued by his superior command. If the mission fails, he's responsible; if the mission succeeds, you also say he's responsible. Now, I'm asking to you, as a former corps commander, whether when we talk about that type of responsibility of a commander, whether this is different from his responsibility which could be engaged if his subordinates, for example, committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the responsibility is different. It's different for a number of reasons. The responsibility of the commander for the failure of the mission generally speaking is his responsibility. But to make myself quite clear, I have to use an example. Because the 3rd Corps commander when forming the corps - and I think this was following the first orders and directives that he received - was given the task -- was given tasks for a non-existent corps to liberate the area of responsibility of the corps as far as the northern border, that is, the Sava River in the north of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then to undertake to lift the blockade around Sarajevo. By giving this example, I wish to say that the corps commander received a mission, was allotted a mission, and he didn't execute it, neither of these two, regardless of whether he received orders from his superior. And now we have a contradiction between his responsibility and the conditions which prevented the commander from accomplishing his mission, the mission assigned to him at the beginning. It's highly questionable whether a NATO corps would be able to carry out such a mission, never mind he with a non-existent corps. Now, if we were to look at that legally, he did not accomplish his mission and he should be held accountable. The fact that he didn't have a corps, that he didn't have ammunition, he didn't have the weapons and the state failed to provide him with all those things that they should have at a level that would be comparable to a NATO corps to be able to carry out that mission, nobody will be held responsible for that. Without pre-empting anything, I'm just trying to put it in my own words. However, if all the resources were not available to him - personnel, equipment, weapons, logistics - and a mission is assigned to him, then to the extent to which those resources were not provided, he cannot be held responsible for the things that were not provided to him. And, on the other hand, if a war crime is committed or a military offence, an act of crime or I don't know what, that is something more direct. That is something more concrete, if I can call it that. But even in that case, when we're talking about the corps commander's responsibility for every disciplinary violation or criminal offence, there is the chain of command. So if a soldier violates discipline, he will first be punished by his superior. It could be company commander or battalion commander. And this is something the corps commander doesn't have to know about. But if it's a criminal offence and it happened in a battalion, in a brigade, then the brigade commander and battalion commander have all the possibilities of instituting proceedings, as does the corps commander or the commander of the operative group. So I'm just emphasising the chain of command, and there are different levels of responsibility within that chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. One more question before we move to the model, when we will invite the Chamber to come down and look at the model. And the question is as follows: At paragraph 604, you say that "the corps commander must avoid being drawn into using his resources to take on activities which, although they may appear important and critical at any given moment, will distract him from his mission." And you also say at paragraph 607 that "At all times a corps commander is expected to give priority to his obligations towards the state and towards his superior; meaning that for a corps commander the mission must always come first." Can you further explain these two paragraphs and apply them to the situation of General Hadzihasanovic from what you've seen in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander is appointed by the Supreme Command, and he's appointed precisely because this is a position of a very high level and rank, and this unit, through various directives from the Supreme Command, is given a mission. And in wartime, in addition to many components of a mission, I would like to point out two basic ones, and that is protection of the territory of one's state -- or rather, defence of the territory of one's state; and protection of the lives of one's soldiers and people. In the execution of his mission, the corps commander is doing his best for the Supreme Command and for the state. However, if in executing that mission the 3rd Corps commander does not have any of the things that he should have as a corps commander -- when I described that position in the Yugoslav People's Army and one of the key issues is that of logistics -- and if he has to daily spend his time, his mental efforts and those of his staff to deal with logistical problems, such as fuel, food, the production of ammunition and weapons, finding the manpower, which is not part of his duty according to the regulations, to the extent to which that has not been provided, to that extent with the quality and the degree of accomplishment of the mission be reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, we have ten minutes left before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is best to have the break now, and we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. The Judges are ready to get up if the Defence so wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. With due respect, I would like to ask the Chamber to be kind enough to approach the model. We have made electronic devices available so that you can each have headsets, and they have been set so that you can hear what the expert is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, if I can ask you -- you should have beside you a microphone and earphones with a long wire which you can wear. And you also have a pointer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I ask whether the three Judges are able to hear the interpretation in their respective languages? Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, this is a first, and we have the Chamber, who can look at this model from close. My first question to you is: Do you recognise this model, what is pictured on this model, and what is indicated or illustrated by the orange wire on the model.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear -- the interpreters can't hear too well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do recognise it. This is a relief of the central part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on this relief this red string symbolically indicates the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I would like you to do at this time, General, is to indicate for the Trial Chamber what was the strategic objectives of the HVO in 1992-1993, and why the area of the 3rd Corps was critical in this respect. I would ask that you point clearly to any towns that you will point with your pointer and that you explain exactly what you can see from this model that can help the Trial Chamber in understanding the situation. So the first question is the strategic objectives of the HVO in 1992-1993. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this is the relief of the area of Central Bosnia which was the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. Let me start from the east. This is the town of Visoko, and it says "Visoko" here. Then the town of Kakanj. It says "Kakanj." This large town here is Zenica. These towns are linked by an important road, which follows the valley of the Bosna River, and that road leads from Sarajevo - this is Sarajevo in the valley here --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, maybe you can get closer on this side so that you can better explain and illustrate.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The city of Sarajevo. Then along the Bosna River Valley, the town of Visoko, then the town of Kakanj, and then the town of Zenica. Moving on, following the Bosna River Valley, the town of Zepce, the town of Zavidovici, and the town of Maglaj, which is mentioned but it is not on the relief. Later on it became part of the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. Here we have the town of Busovaca and the town of Kiseljak, and these two locations are very important. Then the town of Vitez -- I'm sorry, Novi Travnik. Vitez is here. This is Vitez. This is Novi Travnik, and here in the valley is the town of Travnik itself. And over here to the north-west of his area of responsibility is Bugojno. It says "Bugojno" here. And this is Gornji Vakuf. This is the town of Gornji Vakuf. The area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps consists to a great extent of mountainous areas, so that this whole region that I'm pointing to consists of mountains, wooded areas, and inaccessible areas, with a very low population density, a few villages but quite negligible in terms of numbers. The largest population concentration is along the Bosna River Valley and in these towns. And here in this other valley, from Kiseljak via Busovaca, Vitez, and Novi Travnik to Travnik, is another valley. And a third group of towns with large populations is Bugojno and Travnik. In addition to this mountainous region, we also have some large mountains above Zenica, which are linked to the highest mountain in these parts, that is, Mount Vlasic. This is a feature that I'm sure must have been mentioned frequently, and it has a dominant position above Travnik, and then it separates Zenica from the rest. So the only possible directions of contact between Zenica and this part here is -- that is, the Bila Valley, going as far as Travnik, is a road via Ovnak. This is Ovnak here, the pass called Ovnak. And another road via Lasva. And this point is Lasva, a very significant crossroads here. One branch going to Konjic and further on to Travnik. Another large mountainous range is the one I'm showing here, extremely inaccessible and with very small populations. These are just scattered villages in the hills. The only road going from Novi Travnik and linking it to this valley, these two towns, is this road that I pointed to a moment ago, on the annex, and that in fact is a road that the HVO referred to as the "Road of Salvation." As the entire area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, as we have seen in one of the annexes, was part of the large and imagined Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The HVO had planned after the events in Prozor - this is the town of Prozor, here - in October 1991, when by force they took over power and expelled all the Bosniaks and then after December 1991 and January 1992 -- sorry, December 1992 and January 1993, the attacks on Gornji Vakuf, the HVO wanted to cleanse these two towns, as throughout this territory, from the Neretva River, this whole part of the relief was already under the control of the HVO. They wished to occupy Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf, to expel the Bosniak or non-Croat population, to cleanse it ethnically, and along this road to link up with Novi Travnik. And Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak, these four towns were held by the HVO from the very beginning of the war, ever since April 1992: Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez, and Novi Travnik. If we -- if they had taken these two towns, then this whole territory would automatically have become part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. By a simultaneous attack on Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno, the aim was to provoke conflicts in the Bila River Valley, since here, too, there is a large concentration of Bosniak population and especially in the town of Travnik. This point here is known as Turbe. By constant efforts in cooperation with the Army of Republika Srpska operating from Mount Vlasic and acting along this axis and behind these roads, along this axis, if they were to capture Bugojno and Vakuf, Travnik would be almost surrounded, because Novi Travnik and this junction, the point called "T," which was the location of checkpoints, it was constantly under the control of the HVO. And it follows from this that this road along here, that one could take to reach Travnik, the rest are just village roads. And by such provocations, which consisted, among other things, of setting up checkpoints along the roads, the aim being in this valley here to prevent movement of 3rd Corps units. And among other things -- and I am referring to two key checkpoints that were permanently there - they are established here, in Ovnak - this is the road from Zenica to Travnik -- they established these checkpoints, and here in Vitez too. The only two possible directions one could take were through Ovnak and through Vitez. It was possible to come from Vitez to Travnik and return to Zenica from Travnik without being controlled by the 3rd Corps of the ABiH of these two points -- or rather, if it wasn't possible to use the roads in this zone for the corps, it wasn't possible for the corps to move around. That would have prevented logistic supplies, supplying the men, relieving troops. It would have prevented taking the wounded out to Zenica, to the central hospital, et cetera, et cetera. In fact, by imposing a long-term blockade here, this area would have fallen into the hands of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, if I can ask you at this point to indicate where are the Serb forces compared to this area, in addition to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb forces were over here. This was where there was a link between the HVO and the Serbian forces. This is where the first -- the Serbian forces first appeared and they were present along this red line here and as far as Zepce. In Zepce, there was again an enclave of the HVO and they had contact with each other there. And then there were Serbian forces from this point onwards, again, and they extended as far as this point here, roughly speaking. And this is where the 3rd and 2nd Corps in Tuzla linked up, and Tuzla is about here, where I'm standing now. This part, as far as this point, in fact shows the point of contact with the 1st Corps of the ABiH -- or rather, in this area towards the 4th Corps of the ABiH in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, if I can ask you at this point to indicate, if you can, on the model why there was any fighting in Dusina in January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I pointed to Zenica. Then I pointed to Lasva. This is the Lasva junction. A minute ago I said that it was of extreme importance. The village of Dusina is here. I'm pointing to it right now. Let's have a look at Busovaca here, the town of Busovaca, and the town of Kiseljak. Both towns were under the complete control of HVO forces. Kacuni is located here, the small place called Kacuni, at this crossroads here. On the 25th of January, 1993 the commander of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone, the commander of the HVO forces, Tihomir Blaskic, together in coordination with the commander of the North-Western Operations Zone, Stiljek- and these two towns were in his zone - they acted together. Blaskic issued an order from his brigade to Busovaca to attack in the direction of Kacuni to route the 3rd Corps forces in Kacuni and to continue with the attack in the direction of Kiseljak. Kiseljak -- or rather, the Kiseljak Brigade was also issued an order in the same document. The order was to attack from Kiseljak in the direction of Brestovsko, Maljevac, and in the direction of Kacuni. And then this brigade here, this brigade should set off to meet each other. Because in this area that I'm pointing to, from Kacuni to Bilalovac, in this 10-kilometre stretch of territory, the 3rd Corps together with my corps held the separated enclaves of the HVO in Busovaca and the HVO in Kiseljak and Kresevo. This is where these forces of the HVO were separated. Their main objective was to attack from Busovaca and from Kiseljak and to route the 3rd Corps and 1st Corps forces here in order to link up the HVO forces in Busovaca and the HVO forces in Kiseljak and in order to gain control of this road. At the same time, Commander Stiljek, the commander of the Western Herzegovina Operative Zone, attacked Gornji Vakuf, which I pointed to in the annex, so that Gornji Vakuf would fall. They would link up with these towns here, Novi Travnik, Vitez, and if they managed to link up -- if Busovaca and Kiseljak had managed to link up, they would have linked up all the towns together with Kresevo and they would have formed a territory which they called Croatian territory. What was at stake? This attempt, Blaskic's efforts were not to succeed, we weren't to allow him to succeed. Because if he had taken Kacuni, there was an extremely important road through Central Bosnia that went from Kacuni -- or through Kacuni to Sarajevo. There was no other road. And he came from the central part of Bosnia, from Tuzla more or less, and descended to Visoko. That's the way the road goes. And then the road continues through my village, which is here. It descends down to Kacuni, continues to Fojnica. From Fojnica it goes over this hill and over all these hills and arrives here in Tarcin, continues over Igman to Sarajevo and under the tunnel, under the airport, which is here, and reached the town of Sarajevo. Blaskic wanted to cut this road off by issuing his order. I can now provide you with an example. Why did the political and military leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the course of the four years of war never decide to cut off the Serbian corridor from Brcko in the direction of Banja Luka? We don't have the part -- this part of the relief. But I assume that you can imagine a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's because in the central part of Bosnia, Banja Luka, there was a vast stretch of territory under the control of the Serbian forces and they had a link with Belgrade only via a very narrow corridor, near Brcko, and the question that was always posed was: Why don't we cut this corridor off? There is one military rule: Don't touch the enemy in a place that would transform him into a tiger. What does that mean? If they had cut off the Brcko corridor in Banja Luka after a certain amount of time, there would have been either an explosion and the consequences would have been far more negative - it would even be impossible to describe those consequences in terms of the victims - or there would have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a surrender. If that were the case, it would have been good.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with respect to the Lasva junction and Dusina, what were the options of General Hadzihasanovic in order to prevent this from happening and what actually happened? In a few words, looking at the model, please.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just going to deal with that. Blaskic's military mistake was to cut off this road for the ABiH. It would have been cut off here in Kacuni, so that the 3rd Corps commander could prevent the HVO in Busovaca and the HVO in Kiseljak from linking up, he had to send forces from Zenica by using the only road. There was no other road. This is the road he had to use, the road that goes through the Bosna Valley to Lasva and then continues up to here and then via the Dusina village. This was the shortest road to provide Kacuni with assistance, a military-justified action. The consequences are another matter. And this was the reason for which the forces were present here in Dusina. It was in fact to protect Dusina against an HVO attack. And also this village here, the village of Merdani, which is often mentioned in the documents. For General Hadzihasanovic to prevent the forces from linking up and so that he could secure the only road of extreme importance to the ABiH, he did what he did. This was something that was necessary to be done in military terms. It was the only military way of providing assistance and preventing this from happening. The only thing to be done was to send units from the Zenica basin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, my next question deals with the situation in -- in April of 1993 where we know that something took place in the village of Miletici. Can you show where the village of Miletici is in April 1993 and to show if there is any military objective or any reason from a military point of view to have fighting in Miletici in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it now. Is it here? Is this Miletici? The village of Maline, the village of Miletici, on this slope. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It says "Miletici" here. That's the village. When looking at the place and location of the village, the location shows that this village was not and could not be a particular military objective, not for the 3rd Corps of the ABiH, nor for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, General, deals with the situation in June of 1993. Can you show first where is the joint command where the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps was, and that is in the post office in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was in the very centre of the town in Travnik. That's where the commander was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... where General Hadzihasanovic is in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more or less in this area that I'm pointing to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you show where Guca Gora is as well as Velika Bukovica, where the fighting began in June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bukovica -- it says the village of Bukovica here. It's on the slopes of Mount Vlasic. And Guca Gora is over here. I'm not sure that I can see it. It should be in this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I take it from reading your report, General, that you are familiar with the fact that there were a call for assistance from 306 Brigade in the Bila Valley to the 3rd Corps in Zenica, a call for assistance because they were getting into fighting with the HVO. Can you show what were the options at that time if General Hadzihasanovic was to send assistance and what did he decide to do and why.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 306th Brigade is located here, in this zone of responsibility. It was deployed in that area. According to the documents that I had before me, it did send a request for assistance at the beginning of June, just before the 8th of June, 1993. After numerous incidents had occurred and after all the problems that had happened in that area, in Ahmici and throughout the entire valley, for the 3rd Corps commander to intervene and to send any form of assistance, the only way to do that was through Ovnak, or by using this road down here. I think that you can see that it's not possible to pass through these features unless you pass through Divokoze. In order to send assistance, in order for assistance to reach the 306th Brigade and its units in the Bila Valley, there were two options that he had: Either to send assistance via this route, over Ovnak, or via this route, through Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, with respect to those two possibilities, which one of these would have caused more collateral damage or would have been -- inevitably killed more people between those two options?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this route via Vitez had been used, this route -- road here and then the one through Lasva and this entire area along this entire road, well, this area is a very densely inhabited area, so the commander decided to use the other route, which isn't as densely inhabited in comparison to this route here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General --

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terms, the decision was absolutely correct. If I myself had been in such a situation, I would have taken the same decision. That is why he decided to go via Ovnak, to reduce the number of victims and the total collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May I ask, General, in respect of this choice, is this the type of decision that is expected to be made by a corps commander, that is, between two attacks to select the one that will produce the less collateral damage? Is that an operative decision at the corps commander level?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area in question is a very small area, the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. We can see in this relief -- I'm circling the area with this pointer. When you compare this area with the entire zone of responsibility, you can see that it's not at the level of a corps commander. But this doesn't exclude the possibility for a commander to be involved by monitoring what subordinates are doing. This is more or less the task of a brigade, including an operative group at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There may have been some problems with the interpretation, but I have one last question, General, and that is: Can you show that in June of 1993 at the same time as what was happening in the Bila Valley or close thereafter there was other activity in the Zepce area? Can you explain what was the importance of the Zepce, Maglaj, and Zavidovici area in June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 1993, this period was the most difficult, the most critical month for the 3rd Corps of the ABiH. Why? Because of the incessant attacks carried out by the HVO against Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno. Their objective was to break through towards Novi Travnik. And then for a certain period of time there was constant action of the HVO in the Bila Valley. They wanted to place this valley under their control too. And then after January 1993, the HVO was continually trying to join up with its forces from Busovaca and Kiseljak. And in addition to all of this, there was a serious problem in Zepce, where the HVO in Zepce in the course of June prepared an operation to eliminate an entire 3rd Corps brigade. Through the cooperation of the HVO in Zepce and the Republika Srpska army, an agreement was reached that at one point in time they should surrender part of the defence line that they held to the Republika Srpska army in order to separate or single out some of their forces and attack the Zepce Brigade of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH and to take and establish full control over the entire town of Zepce. On the 30th of June, 1993 - that's what it says in the documents - they did this. On the 1st of July, 1993, Ivo Lozancic, the top political HVO leader in Zepce, reported to the 3rd Corps commander, sent him a document, and informed him that there are three and a half thousand civilians that had been captured and a thousand soldiers from that brigade who had surrendered. About four and a half thousand people were placed in a tunnel. There's a big tunnel in the vicinity of Zepce. And he asked them -- he asked General Hadzihasanovic so as not to continue shelling, et cetera, he asked for an exchange to be organised as soon as possible because he couldn't provide these four and a half thousand people with the necessary conditions in that tunnel. The brigade commander and most of the brigade members were captured. Only a small part to have brigade managed to break out and join other 3rd Corps brigades. When you observe this at the level of the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, the cooperation of the HVO and the Republika Srpska army, when you bear in mind the incessant attacks on Zenica and the fact that there was cooperation of the VRS and the HVO here and incessant attacks carried out on Travnik, there were incessant incidents and fighting within the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, there was the attack on Bugojno and Vakuf, on Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf. There was an attack between Busovaca and Kiseljak, and then there were the problems of the HVO at the beginning in Kakanj - the town of Kakanj is here - this shows that the 3rd Corps of the ABiH in 1993, in the summer of 1993, and its commander were an impossible situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know if the Judges would like to ask questions now or whether we could perhaps see the model next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, General. If we can go back. We will go back and now see the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, General. We will now look at Annex 74. I would like you to explain what is Annex 74 and how we can from Annex 74 see the difficult situation of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole but especially the 3rd Corps. And you may use the pencil if you would like.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This annex depicts Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the legend shows three different colours. Red stands for the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in January 1993 under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. The yellow shows the part of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the control of the Croatian Defence Council. And the blue shows the part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was under the control of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I shall point to the yellow enclave of Zepce. I shall encircle it in red. The next enclave is Vares, and the next one is Kiseljak and Kresevo. Kiseljak and Kresevo. Here they are. And this larger enclave, Busovaca, is this. Vitez is here. And Novi Travnik, here. Then we have the enclave of Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf, which wasn't an enclave but is on the very line of conflict with the HVO. Gornji Vakuf is here. This part of the territory between Busovaca and Kiseljak was what needed to be cut across, and I am indicating this in a thick red line. This was -- would mean the main bloodstream for the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and for anyone who wanted to come from Tuzla or Zenica, to the south, or to Sarajevo, that was the route he would have to use. We mentioned the village of Dusina. The next slide which follows on to the previous one, we see what happened. We have another colour now. In the north-west of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the left-hand corner, this territory was captured by Fikret Abdic and his forces, that is, the north-western part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So a new enemy cropped up for the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Because the previous annex referred to January 1993, and this one, this slide, which follows on to the previous one, reflects the state of affairs in December 1993. Now we have another colour as well, and to the east, where the blue indicates the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the forces of Republika Srpska occupied this entire territory during 1993. So in Brcko we have a part of the territory, and I am encircling it now. Then south of Kalesija, also some territory. Around Srebrenica and Zepa, this whole area here. Around Visegrad, again areas they occupied. What remains was Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. I am placing red dots in these three blue enclaves. So then the links between Gorazde and Sarajevo were cut across. Then there's an area near Kladanj and Zivinice. In six or seven different places forces of the Army of Republika Srpska in 1993 gained control and occupied more territory. What am I saying? I wish to say that the year 1993 from the strategic standpoint for the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was a turning point. It was the most difficult year because the Croatian Defence Council and the Army of Republika Srpska had agreed together with Fikret Abdic, in the north-west of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and according to that agreement they split up their responsibilities, so that the Army of Republika Srpska said, "I will occupy the whole area along the eastern border of Bosnia and Herzegovina," which they in fact did, with the exception of three small enclaves: Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, which really didn't mean anything strategically. The HVO was given the task within the area that had been proclaimed as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to occupy all those places that I pointed to on the model, and together with Fikret Abdic, who managed to destroy the 5th Corps in the north-west of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I have to interrupt you because we only have a ten minutes left and I have a couple of slides that --

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one more sentence, if I may. Had this preconceived plan been fulfilled, all that would have remained of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and all its corps, only perhaps five, six, or seven small enclaves, which eventually would have had to fall and surrender, capitulate. Fortunately, this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to move to Annex 80 on page 2. If you can quickly show what you showed on the map concerning the plan of the HVO to link up Busovaca and Kiseljak. If you can indicate where Zenica is.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zenica is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You also have other colours you can use. There's a black you can use. Maybe it would be better. If you can indicate where Zenica is.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zenica is here. I've just put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and where is Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Busovaca is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where Kiseljak is, or at least the direction towards Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kiseljak is in the bottom right-hand corner, south of this rectangle that I have drawn. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Where Kacuni is.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kacuni is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the Lasva junction?

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lasva is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where the line of advance of the forces being sent to defend through Dusina from Zenica to Dusina to Kacuni, what you explained earlier.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can draw a line of the route from Zenica via the Lasva junction and via Dusina to assist Kacuni. This is this blue line. And it is the only possible route.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you just say where Dusina is.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusina is about here, where I've drawn the circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you write beside "Dusina." We will try to freeze this picture for later.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move to another annex, which is Annex 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I can obtain ten more minutes, because tomorrow we won't have this computer technology in Courtroom II, so if I could use this extra time to show the three remaining maps.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This annex shows the direction of attack from Busovaca towards Kiseljak. This is Kiseljak. The dot I have put a circle around in red. And this is Busovaca, and this is the direction of attack to Kiseljak and vice versa, from Kiseljak to Busovaca, with the aim of linking up these two enclaves. At the same time, there were constant attempts via Gornji Vakuf to link up these enclaves and the enclave of Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] I'd like to move now to Annex 111, which deals with the situation in June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not so much the difficulty. It is that the picture is very large. The slide is -- the file is a very thick one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, can you please quickly describe what we see on this annex.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This annex shows in red the line of the forces of Republika Srpska. It goes to the north-east. The blue dotted line are the defence lines of the 3rd Corps of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the same time, these roads are drawn in brown and there are a large number of checkpoints along those roads. The town of Travnik I think can be seen well, is here; Nova Travnik, Vitez, and Zenica. All these checkpoints are not as important as the three key checkpoints, and they are the following: This one, at Ovnak, that I pointed to on the relief a moment ago; this checkpoint here, in Vitez, that I also pointed to on the model; and this checkpoint, at the junction mentioned as "T". These three checkpoints are of key significance, and it is only through them that it is possible to enter the Bila Valley. All three of these checkpoints, as shown by the legend, are held by the HVO. The black dotted line is the border of Travnik municipality, and if you look at all these checkpoints, including those held by the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, indicates how complicated the situation in the area was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's now move to Annex 112, which is the before-last annex, which shows the attack on Ovnak. In the meantime, General, I have one question for you, and that is: The importance of linking up Vares on one side to, on the other side, where we have Zepce, Maglaj, and Zavidovici, how important that was for the VRS from a strategic point of view in June and July of 1993.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand the question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then maybe, General, we will just go on this map and then I'll show you the other annex. I was just trying to make some time. Can you explain what is happening on this annex, which is 112.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Annex 112 shows the mutual deployment on the 8th of June, 1993. Again, we have the colours. The blue stands for the forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; the red, for the VRS; the brown, for the Croatian Defence Council. Actually, behind this red dotted line, this territory that I'm marking is controlled by the VRS. This colour is controlled by the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this one here, by the HVO. Actually, the black dotted line is the border of the Travnik municipality, and the blue dotted line, the 3rd Corps of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This part here - and I'm going to try and circle it in blue - is an enclave of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Another enclave; a third here; a fourth here; and of course this area up here was controlled by the ABiH, that is, the 3rd Corps. All the territory in between, the largest percentage was controlled by the HVO. Ovnak, the place we mentioned, is right here. And the other point, Vitez, is about here. The commander decided to use the route via Ovnak, and we tried to show this -- show the axis of direction -- the axis of the attacks of the units within the newly formed Tactical Group Ovnak, which was formed due to the request for assistance received from the 306th Brigade. This brigade that I am putting a circle round. The aim of this battle was for this part here to -- that I have marked with a black line, to remove the checkpoint at Ovnak, to deblock the road via Ovnak, so as to provide assistance to these enclaves that I am ticking off. These three, and especially the Travnik enclave. All of this started on the 8th of June, 1993, and after that a completely new line of separation was established between the 3rd Corps of the ABiH and the HVO, which is shown in another annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We'll move to the last annex, which is Annex 74, to show the -- what was happening in the Maglaj finger. Can you explain quickly, General, what was -- what happened here in terms of the yellow part around Maglaj and from Vares to Zavidovici, what was the interest of the VRS to link Vares and Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need a map of the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the VRS as well had a similar interest as the HVO to link Busovaca and Kiseljak, so the VRS wanted to link with its forces via Olovo to the area of Zavidovici, et cetera. By linking up the forces of the VRS from Podlug and Olovo, the Tuzla region would be totally cut off and turned into an enclave. It would be physically cut off from the Zenica region. As a result, the 2nd and 3rd Corps would be physically separated. That's one matter. And in that respect, the interests of Zepce and Vares coincide. Luckily that is not what happened, because my corps fought -- had heavy battles in Olovo for some three months to defend Olovo and not allow Serb forces to break through via Olovo and link up with their own forces and thus transforming Tuzla into an enclave. However, when talking about Zepce, as I said on the 30th of June -- or rather, the 1st of July, 1993, the HVO, this area marked in yellow - I am ticking it off or making a circle in it - they had agreed with the VRS to surrender a part to have front, some positions. And I shall try to mark those positions in black. This is those -- where those positions were. I'm showing it in -- with a black arrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, could you indicate --

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: So by agreement between the VRS and the HVO, the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had another enclave, Maglaj and Tesanj, because it was cut off from the rest, which was another very difficult problem as to how to fight in Tesanj and Maglaj, how to communicate with them, how to supply food and resupply them with ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... black marker, indicate the link-up between what was being tried with Vares and Olovo to link it up to the other side to see what would have been the result.

utterances.speaker: Vahid Karavelic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall mark it in red. The forces of the aggressor, of the VRS, tried together with the HVO to attack in this direction, and they also attacked from this direction. And then together they wanted to physically prevent contact between the 2nd and the 3rd Corps, and with me too, because the 2nd Corps was physically linked to the 3rd and to my corps. Then Tuzla would have become an enclave, another enclave. That's one. And I want to use this map to show something else. The attempts between Busovaca and Kiseljak - and I am drawing a new red line - they wanted to link up here too, and this shows that the whole of the territory under the control of the ABiH would be cut up into five or six enclaves, which could hardly survive on their own and would disappear with time and so would Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state, after which the UN would probably have to pass a new resolution annulling the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you for the additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll adjourn for today. General, you will come back tomorrow. That will begin at 9.00 in the morning. Thank you all. And we meet again tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.
